c.tagline: Where Atlantic surf meets Africa's oil-boom energy.

taxi.fareNote: Formal metered taxis are rare; fares for regular taxis and candongueiro minibuses are fixed/negotiated in advance, so agree the price before you get in or use a ride-hailing app.

emergency.note: Emergency response can be slow and inconsistent; save your hotel's or embassy's security contact as a backup, and note the fire brigade line is 115.

hood_landmark.Ilha de Luanda: Ilha de Luanda beach strip, Luanda

avoid.reason: High crime and very expensive; caution at night; keep car doors locked; petty theft

hood_desc: A narrow sandy peninsula lined with beach clubs, seafood shacks and nightlife just across the bay from downtown; suits travelers who want a beach-and-party base close to the center.

A sprawling modern business district of gated condominiums, malls and the convention center; suits business travelers wanting new infrastructure and 24-hour security, at the cost of a long commute downtown.
An exclusive diplomatic and residential enclave along the Marginal bay with sweeping ocean views; favored by executives and diplomats wanting Luanda's most upscale hotels.
A quieter, tree-lined residential area popular with expat families and longer stays, within easy reach of the Kinaxixi market and central Luanda.
The historic downtown core packed with colonial-era buildings, government offices, the old fortress and the Marginal promenade; best for first-time visitors who want to walk to the main sights.
lodging: Guesthouse Mobilada na Ilha de Luanda
Talatona Convention Hotel (Hotel de Convenções de Talatona)

water.note: Tap water is not safe to drink; stick to bottled water.

transit.pay: Fares on buses and candongueiros are paid in cash (kwanza) directly to the driver or conductor; there is no citywide contactless card system. The CFL commuter train sells paper tickets at stations. Most visitors avoid public buses altogether and use ride-hailing apps or hotel-arranged drivers instead.
transit.hours: Buses and candongueiros generally run roughly 5am-9pm; service is sparse after dark, so taxis or ride-hailing apps are the practical option at night.
transit.note: Public transport is crowded and informally run rather than tourist-oriented; most visitors rely on private drivers, hotel transfers or the Yango app.

airport.name: Dr. António Agostinho Neto International Airport (NBJ)
airport.drive: 45-70 min via the new six-lane highway, depending on traffic

tip.r: Tipping is not traditional in Angola, but 5-10% is appreciated at upscale restaurants and hotels catering to business travelers; rounding up is common for taxis.

food.name: Muamba de galinha
food.desc: Angola's national dish: chicken simmered with red palm oil, okra, garlic and gindungo chilli, eaten with funge or rice.

places.name: Cais de Quatro
places.note: Iconic Luanda restaurant blending Mediterranean cooking with Angolan classics.

places.name: La Vigia
places.note: Unfussy, lively local favourite known for cooking the Angolan way, not for tourists.

places.name: Espaco Bahia
places.note: Beachfront spot popular with Luandans for traditional plates and weekend music.

food.name: Calulu
food.desc: Dried and fresh fish (or beef) stewed with sweet potato leaves, okra, tomato and palm oil, layered slowly and served over funge.

places.name: Lookal Mar
places.note: Seafood favourite whose kitchen turns out calulu and moamba alongside fresh fish.

places.name: Cais de Quatro
places.note: Reliable, well-reviewed version of calulu in a smart waterfront setting.

places.name: La Vigia
places.note: Where regulars go for flavour over fanfare; generous traditional portions.

food.name: Funge and pirao
food.desc: The staple starch: cassava flour (funge de bombo) or maize meal stirred to a smooth, stretchy mound and used to scoop up stews by hand.

places.name: La Vigia
places.note: Serves proper cassava funge with its stews, the way locals order it.

places.name: Espaco Bahia
places.note: Traditional beachside kitchen; funge comes with calulu, muamba or grilled fish.

places.name: Mercado do Benfica
places.note: Big market with cooked-food stalls doing funge and stew at local prices.

food.name: Mufete
food.desc: Luanda's weekend ritual: grilled fish with beans in palm oil, boiled cassava, sweet potato, fried ripe banana and a fierce onion-chilli relish.

places.name: Espaco Bahia
places.note: Classic Ilha mufete with your feet close to the sand; busiest on Sundays.

places.name: Chill Out
places.note: Long-running beach restaurant-bar, a Luanda standard for mufete and sunsets.

places.name: La Vigia
places.note: Charcoal-kissed seafood served Angolan style, mufete included.

food.name: Grelhados de marisco (grilled seafood)
food.desc: Ilha do Cabo runs on charcoal-grilled prawns, lobster, garoupa and carapau, dressed with lemon, garlic and gindungo pepper sauce.

places.name: Lookal Mar
places.note: Favourite for fresh fish and lobster with sunset views over the bay.

places.name: Cais de Quatro
places.note: One of Luanda's best-known seafood addresses; book at weekends.

places.name: Chill Out
places.note: Casual beach setting for grilled prawns and cold Cuca.

food.name: Cocada amarela and doce de ginguba
food.desc: Portuguese-Angolan sweets: golden coconut and egg-yolk pudding scented with cinnamon, plus chewy peanut brittle sold on the street.

places.name: Cais de Quatro
places.note: Keeps traditional Angolan desserts on the menu alongside Mediterranean dishes.

places.name: Espaco Bahia
places.note: Home-style cocada amarela after a mufete lunch.

places.name: Mercado do Benfica
places.note: Stalls sell doce de ginguba and coconut sweets to take away cheaply.

food.name: Cuca and N Gola beer
food.desc: Cuca is Angola's flagship lager and a national symbol; N Gola and Eka are the local rivals. All are drunk very cold with grilled seafood.

places.name: Chill Out
places.note: Beach bar where an ice-cold Cuca at sunset is the whole point.

places.name: Coconuts
places.note: Popular Ilha bar for late drinks and live music by the water.

places.name: Cais de Quatro
places.note: Full bar with cold beer and cocktails to go with the seafood.

food.name: Mukua juice and kissangua
food.desc: Mukua is tangy baobab-fruit juice, sold chilled and sometimes as ice lollies; kissangua is a lightly fermented maize drink from the interior.

places.name: Mercado do Benfica
places.note: Best place to find mukua, ginguba and other traditional drinks made locally.

places.name: Espaco Bahia
places.note: Serves fresh tropical juices, including baobab, with traditional meals.

places.name: La Vigia
places.note: Local-leaning menu where natural juices sit next to the beer list.

landmarks: Fortress of São Miguel
This 16th-century Portuguese fortress crowns a hill above the bay, housing a fascinating military history museum and offering sweeping views over Luanda's skyline.
Agostinho Neto Mausoleum
A soaring 120-metre rocket-shaped monument built with Soviet help, this striking memorial to Angola's first president dominates the Luanda skyline day and night.
Iron Palace (Palácio de Ferro)
This elegant prefabricated iron structure, rumored to be designed by Gustave Eiffel's workshop, is a delicate architectural curiosity transported piece by piece from Europe.
Luanda Bay & Marginal Promenade
The city's glittering waterfront boulevard curves along the crescent bay, lined with palm trees and skyscrapers, making it Luanda's most photographed cityscape at sunset.
Ilha do Cabo (Luanda Island)
This narrow sandy peninsula separating the bay from the Atlantic is packed with lively beach bars, seafood restaurants, and postcard views back toward the mainland skyline.
National Bank of Angola building
A grand colonial-era edifice in the historic downtown, this landmark bank building showcases ornate architecture that reflects Luanda's layered Portuguese heritage.
National Slavery Museum
Set in a former colonial chapel overlooking the bay, this sobering museum preserves artifacts documenting the transatlantic slave trade that once passed through this coastline.
Church of Our Lady of Remedies (Luanda Cathedral)
One of Luanda's oldest surviving churches, this whitewashed cathedral facade in the historic quarter blends Baroque colonial style with centuries of local history.
Miradouro da Lua (Moon Viewpoint)
A dramatic lunar-like landscape of eroded cliffs and canyons about 40 km south of the city, this otherworldly viewpoint is a favorite day trip for striking photography.
Kalandula Falls
Among Africa's largest waterfalls, this thundering 105-metre curtain of water in Malanje province draws travelers willing to venture beyond the capital for an awe-inspiring sight.

train.note: No international trains: Angola's three railways are not linked to each other or across borders (the DRC-facing Benguela Railway starts far south at Lobito and is freight-focused). From Luanda, CFL runs one daily long-distance train inland to Malanje via Dondo, plus busy commuter trains to Viana. There is no online booking - buy tickets at the Bungo/Baía station in Luanda; CFL's Facebook page is its main channel for timetables.

bus.note: Macon runs a long-haul international coach from Luanda to Windhoek, Namibia (about three departures a week), crossing at the Santa Clara/Oshikango border - a very long ride, so carry your passport and a Namibian visa if required. Crossings toward the DR Congo are mostly informal shared taxis rather than scheduled coaches.

ferry.note: No scheduled international passenger ferries. Domestically, coastal boats connect Luanda and the Cabinda exclave with Soyo in the north (operators include Secil Marítima and TMA Express), which is a common way to reach Cabinda without transiting DR Congo. Services can be irregular, so check current sailings locally before relying on them.

full.name: N’dalatando
full.blurb: Agricultural town in northern Angola known for coffee and lush tropical landscapes.
